newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worried by rapid rise in Japanese car imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worried by rapid rise in Japanese car imports.

text.p: U.S. trade officials expressed concern on Friday about rising Japanese car imports into the U.S. market and said Tokyo needed to do more to open Japan's markets to U.S. car products.

In an assessment of a hard-fought 1995 car trade agreement between the two countries, U.S. trade officials said progress has generally been positive. But they expressed disappointment in the pace of deregulation of Japan's car parts markets and in the low number of dealerships that have agreed to sell U.S.-made cars in Japan.

"We are pleased that progress continues to be made under the agreement," U.S. Secretary of Commerce William Daley said in a statement. "U.S. vehicle sales in Japan jumped 34 percent and exports of U.S.-made automotive parts rose to $2 billion in 1996, an increase of 20 percent over 1995."

But U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said that despite market access gains last year, she was concerned about developing trade trends. She cited concerns about rising Japanese car imports in the U.S. market during the first three months of the year.

"We don't want to see a significant increase in the Japanese trade surplus," Barshefsky said. "The overall imbalance in U.S.-Japan auto trade and the first quarter surge in Japanese imports requires that we watch this situation closely."

The report said Japanese dealers have been reluctant to agree to sell U.S.-made cars and only 114 new dealer outlets have been added by the Big Three U.S. automakers since the car trade agreement was signed. The report also said more deregulation was needed in Japan's parts markets to provide opportunities for U.S. parts manufacturers. The car trade agreement was signed in 1995 after the two countries neared the brink of a tit-for-tat trade war over the issue.
